NEW YORK, Oct 13 : Apple on Tuesday unveiled a smart-home hub that taps iPhone user data to make Siri more personal, but promised privacy safeguards designed to keep that information out of the company's hands. The HomeView smart-home hub, which took center stage at an event in New York, is an important test of Apple's AI strategy as it tries to close the gap with rivals Amazon and Alphabet's Google, while reinforcing its reputation for user privacy. In a series of demonstrations, Apple showed Siri AI recognizing a user's face and performing personalized tasks such as fetching recipes from text messages, finding a nearby farmer's market for missing ingredients and then updating shopping lists.  When a different member of the household steps in, the HomeView recognizes that user's face and switches to their personal data, for example fetching information from text messages about when a friend's early morning flight lands and how long it will take them to arrive, then teeing up a coffee maker a few minutes ahead of time.

The new device and Siri AI lean on the iPhone to make those personalized features happen, reflecting new CEO John Ternus' vision of Apple's best-selling product as an "intelligent personal hub" laid out at Apple's iPhone launch event last month.  Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user. HomeView draws on a personal search index stored on the user's iPhone to personalize responses. "That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview. PRIVACY SAFEGUARDS AND ENCRYPTION HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip. To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself. Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts. "One of the things we talked about is not building a marketing profile," Drance said. "Our intent is to provide users a helpful experience that adheres to simplicity, being personal, being intelligent, and continuing our commitment to privacy." A key difference between Siri AI and rival systems is that it does not end each interaction with a follow-up question designed to elicit more information from the user, a practice that Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, said was a deliberate choice on Apple's part.  "For us, it's really about creating these really great products for consumers, which is why we're not in this game of getting you to engage and continue the conversation in many, many, many turns," Rincon said. HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen. Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work. While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user. "There is a logic built in to kind of manage that experience," Drance said. "There was thought put into the nature of that communal computer sharing of the voice and the face recognition."

Source: Reuters

Oct 13 : US carrier AT&T on Tuesday said it has agreed to sell its Mexican unit to Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings for $2 billion in cash, as it sharpens its focus on domestic fiber and 5G networks. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending regulatory approvals in Mexico, AT&T said in a statement. Its Mexican unit, the country's second-largest mobile operator, had approximately 24.7 million subscribers as of December 2025, according to Televisa. • The deal's purchase price of $2 billion in cash is subject to adjustments, plus additional contractual and contingent benefits, and will be funded through available cash and non-recourse secured debt financing. • Televisa and Fintech each own a 50 per cent stake of the consortium that is purchasing AT&T.

Oct 13 : US federal agents arrested a Saudi national employed as an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. OpenAI had used its internal AI models to identify the individual responsible for planting the device and to trace its origins, it said in an X post. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," according to the AI company. The company said it referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The FBI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for more details.

OpenAI faces scrutiny over security incidents involving its AI systems. FAST

FRANKFURT, Oct 13 : The increased use of AI by euro zone companies could curb workers' ability to demand higher wages while heavy investment into the new technology may be materially tightening financing conditions, ECB chief economist Philip Lane said on Tuesday. With inflation now running at nearly twice the ECB's 2 per cent target on expensive energy, policymakers are searching for signs of second-round price effects, but have so far concluded there are none, especially in wage growth. While AI has not changed employment trends, hiring plans are muted and this limits workers' ability to demand compensation for high inflation, Lane said, offering a potential explanation for why wage growth is slowing, despite high inflation. "The potential for AI to replace some types of workers may also weaken the bargaining power of workers, moderating wage growth and reducing the labour share in total income," Lane said in a speech in Dublin.

While Lane did not directly discuss current monetary policy, he said that companies around the globe are borrowing so heavily to fund AI that this is pushing up borrowing costs for everyone and tightening financing conditions by a rate that is now relevant for ECB policy. "The spillover to the euro area bond market means that the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area," Lane said. "This is a relevant factor for the ECB in determining the appropriate monetary policy stance." The comments are significant since the ECB has been raising interest rates to prevent inflation from getting embedded and tighter overall financing conditions could mean the ECB may need to do less to tame price growth, some economists say. AI could also have a relevant impact for the economy over the longer term, raising potential output and trend growth, which would increase the economy's potential 'speed limit,' Lane said. "For Europe, the potential for AI to offset the economic impact of the projected trend decline in the working-age population is especially valuable," he said.

Source: Reuters

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 13 : More than two dozen lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration to pause the use of a new AI tool in the Washington area to assist air traffic controllers, citing safety concerns. The lawmakers, including Democratic Representatives April Delaney, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Don Beyer, said in a letter they were concerned with the FAA pilot project "as we have not seen any safety evaluation and testing reports, nor have we been made aware of any efforts to train aviation safety personnel on how best to use the tool." The letter seeks an answer by Oct. 19. "Air traffic control leaves zero margin for error," Ocasio-Cortez said Tuesday, calling for the pause. The FAA last month began using a new software-based AI tool system that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed.

"We are deeply concerned about the integration of any AI-enabled system into air traffic control systems, where decisions are literally a matter of life or death," said the letter that was also signed by Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representatives Jamie Raskin, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Kweisi Mfume. The FAA in June awarded an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence for a system dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories or SMART, which uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur. The FAA is initially using the AI tool in the airspace around Washington, D.C. and plans to gradually expand it to other parts of the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Tuesday called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge - not the software. "Air traffic controllers will always control the airspace. This is just giving additional tools for controllers to better manage" weather and other issues," Duffy said on Fox Business' "Big Money in the Morning." The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky, USDOT said. "It's going to be transformational," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters earlier. "We'll make much better decisions if we have better decision-making tools." The plan is to initially use it to more effectively reschedule flights that were canceled due to bad weather with plans to expand to other tasks such as strategically coordinating schedules and trajectories before aircraft depart.

Source: Reuters

FAST

WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 13 : Chip technology supplier Arm Holdings breached a licensing agreement with Qualcomm and intentionally interfered with the chipmaker's business relationship with Meta Platforms, a Delaware jury found on Tuesday, but awarded nominal damages of just $2. The verdict followed a five-day trial last week, the second in two years between the companies, that highlighted the deterioration of their business relationship after SoftBank Group acquired control of Arm in 2016 and Arm shifted from licensing the technology needed to make chips to selling chips of its own. Shares of Arm were down 1 per cent following the verdict, while shares of Qualcomm rose 1 per cent, although its stock was down slightly from gains of around 2.4 per cent before the verdict. Both companies welcomed aspects of the verdict, which leaves some key issues unresolved.

"We are gratified that the jury found Arm breached its long-standing Architectural License Agreement (ALA) with Qualcomm, failed to honor its commitments, and intentionally acted to disrupt Qualcomm's businesses," Qualcomm said in a statement. Arm said that "despite Qualcomm’s pursuit of this case in an attempt to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury’s verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only two dollars confirms the merit of Arm’s arguments in the case." The jury found Arm breached its obligation to provide software patches and tools for its designs. The jury found for Arm on five other breach allegations. The jury also found that Arm intentionally and negligently interfered with Qualcomm's relations with Meta. Qualcomm claimed it had been on the cusp of a deal with Meta in 2024 when Arm allegedly leaked to Bloomberg News that Qualcomm had breached a licensing agreement, delaying the Meta agreement. While the jury awarded a nominal $1 for each of those claims, the findings also keep open Qualcomm's claims ahead of the lawsuit's next phase, in which US District Judge Maryellen Noreika must resolve several disputes. The breach finding leaves open the possibility that Noreika could rule that as a result, Qualcomm can stop paying royalties to Arm for five years, potentially worth billions of dollars. Arm has argued the five-year royalty penalty, which is contained in a clause in the licensing agreement, is unenforceable. The business interference finding by the jury could be used by Qualcomm to support its narrative that Arm refused to negotiate in good faith for Arm's next version of its technology, which the judge also must resolve.  The losing side in those decisions would likely appeal.

Source: Reuters

Oct 13 : Alphabet's Google on Wednesday released its flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon to developers and businesses worldwide, seeking to regain ground against rivals OpenAI and Anthropic after months of delays and a leadership shakeup at its DeepMind lab.  The model excels at "deep work" on complex, multi-step tasks in coding, finance, law, cybersecurity and science, Google said. API pricing at launch starts at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with rates set to double after November 30.  The release follows a rocky stretch in Google's AI efforts. The company announced in September that it no longer planned to release Gemini 3.5 Pro, which CEO Sundar Pichai had originally said would be released in June. It also overhauled DeepMind after the AI lab's co-founder and CEO Demis Hassabis stepped aside and several leaders of its Gemini model left the company.

Argon is available to paying customers through the company's AI application building tools. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can access it through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, while the Antigravity coding tool is limited to Ultra subscribers. Teams using Argon in Antigravity increased agentic code submissions by more than 35 per cent, while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third, Google said.   Customers testing the model early include Deloitte, LexisNexis, Ambience Healthcare and Isomorphic Labs. Meanwhile, Google said it would open its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners. The program gives vetted cybersecurity defenders a version of Argon without its cyber guardrails. In September, the company had said it was providing the model to select cybersecurity partners. Separately, Google will offer 10,000 scientists six months of free access to Antigravity's highest usage tier.

WASHINGTON, Oct 13 : A US Senate committee report released on Tuesday said consultants who assist schools and libraries in winning funding from a $3 billion annual internet subsidy program receive between $200 million and $400 million annually. Senate Commerce Committee chair Ted Cruz said consultants help the applicants for the Federal Communications Commission E-Rate program "comply with a Byzantine process that has become a costly feature of the program."  He added that the high fees should "prompt greater scrutiny of how E-Rate funds move, who benefits and whether the program's current structure delivers value to schools, libraries and taxpayers." The FCC has been subsidizing connectivity to and within schools for almost 30 years.

The report found that some consultants charge school districts $100,000 or more per year. Milwaukee Public Schools has participated in E-Rate for more than two decades and has received more than $115 million in funding but is still paying more than $250,000 annually in consulting services, the report said. "The continued need for significant consultant support raises questions about the extent to which long-term participants remain dependent on outside expertise to navigate the program," the report said. The school district and the FCC did not immediately comment. The report added that the consultants are subject to limited oversight and cited a number of criminal cases in E-Rate fraud cases and recommended the FCC require public disclosure of consultant compensation associated with E-Rate and urged the commission to stop expansion of E-Rate until its vulnerabilities are addressed. In June, FCC Chair Brendan Carr said the commission was launching a comprehensive review of the E-Rate program, adding that it could reform the scheme or end it. The FCC is reviewing whether the program has fulfilled its mission and whether continued funding is consistent with Congress' objective. E-Rate is funded by fees paid by telecom companies that are collected from consumers through the "Universal Service Fee" on monthly phone bills.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 13 : Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said on Tuesday it would be interesting to watch for political volatility around AI centers ahead of midterm elections. Speaking at an analysts' call for quarterly earnings, he also said as the financing needs for AI projects grow and there is pressure on rates, it could affect the returns and the viability of certain projects. "Localized political volatility around data centers. You know, we've got an election coming up. It'll be interesting to see," Solomon said. "Obviously there's a lot of political discussion coming into an election, but then you also have to see how states and localities act coming out of elections. All these things can create you know volatility, and there's uncertainty around them."

Data centers, which provide the computing power needed to train and run AI models, have faced growing opposition from communities across the United States. Residents have raised concerns about their rising electricity demand, the potential for higher utility bills and other environmental impacts on local communities. The artificial intelligence buildout is on track to require a larger share of U.S. output than the rollout of electricity, railroads, interstate highways or the internet, with an increasingly complicated financial structure that poses potentially systemic risks, according to a new study. The expansion will consume around 3.6 per cent of gross domestic product annually through 2032, or more than $10 trillion, and is using ever more intricate financing arrangements, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a finance and real estate professor at Columbia Business School, wrote in a paper prepared for a Brookings Institution conference last month. "There's going to be infrastructure built around it that's going to be quite significant," Goldman's Solomon. "But we feel very well positioned to bring the full range of services and participate actively, and we still see an enormous amount of activity." Goldman is a financial partner with Nvidia, which in August announced it has partnered with six major financial institutions to launch compute platforms aimed at raising over $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure.

Oct 13 : Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee said on Tuesday that inflation is starting to feel like "aggregate overheating" fueled by spillovers from the artificial intelligence investment boom rather than largely being a byproduct of supply shocks that will pass on its own. "This is starting to feel like aggregate overheating, that the AI data center cost increases are jumping out of its lane, that prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries to data centers," Goolsbee said in a Semafor interview. "If you start to see more of this spreading into general services, that investment goods are just getting GDP (gross domestic product) growth up faster than potential and generating this kind of spillover inflation, that’s problematic because unlike supply shocks where we tend to assume they’re going to go away on their own in a relatively short period of time, nobody thinks that of overheating demand." "It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that," Goolsbee said. "So that’s why the conventional wisdom among economists has been if you see overheating demand, you act decisively and you act quickly to prevent that from rolling into inflation expectations, rolling into people taking for granted that it’s never going to go away." Asked whether the Fed should continue raising interest rates, Goolsbee, who does not have a vote on rate policy this year, said: "So if inflation remains persistent, then I think it’s clear what the Fed has to do. If we can get some evidence that this tariff inflation is going away, that the oil shock inflation is going away, it’s not too much progress that we need to show, but we need to start showing some progress if we’re going to get back on the kind of rate cutting path that we were on." The Fed cut rates three times in 2025 but last month raised rates for the first time in three years in the face of stubborn inflation, bumping its short-term policy rate up by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent. Rate futures markets expect it will forego another increase at the coming October 27-28 meeting but will lift rates by another quarter point in December.

Source: Reuters

Oct 13 : Hyundai Motor Group said on Tuesday it would invest $15.5 billion in India through 2032, deepening its bet on the world's third-largest car market as a key driver of future growth.  The South Korean automaker's seven-year plan includes about $700 million of investment in its Indian research and development centre, expansion of production capacity and a dedicated investment entity. India, the world's third-largest car market, is attracting billions of dollars in investment from global automakers seeking to tap rising demand and expand local manufacturing capacity, underscoring its position as a major automotive production hub.  Hyundai said last year it would invest $5 billion to expand its manufacturing and research operations in India.

Japan's Suzuki Motor , the majority owner of India's largest carmaker by volume, Maruti Suzuki, also laid out plans in 2025 to invest about $8 billion in the country. Carmakers such as Toyota and Honda have committed to expanding their manufacturing ambitions in India as well.  Hyundai Motor, which employs more than 24,000 people in India, said the investment would create additional jobs across manufacturing, research, engineering and supply chains, but did not disclose a number.  The firm said the investment plan, covering 2026 to 2032, would expand manufacturing capacity at Hyundai Motor India and Kia India to support significant volume growth. The investment also includes a vehicle testing track, as part of efforts to develop next-generation automotive technologies. The investment announcement followed a meeting between Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Tuesday. The group currently has an annual production capacity of more than 1.4 million vehicles in India, comprising 824,000 units at Hyundai's Chennai facilities, 170,000 units at its Pune plant and 431,000 units at Kia's Anantapur facility.

AMSTERDAM, Oct 13 : Dutch supermarket company Ahold Delhaize has no indication that client data has been stolen in the cybersecurity incident that forced it to shut down several systems in recent days, it said in a statement on Tuesday. The Dutch retailer, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in other European countries as well as the United States, said on Monday that it was dealing with a "security issue" on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution. The incident coincided with a cyberattack in France which saw refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of stores heating up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, sparking fires and spoiling food. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre has said that there is no reason to believe that there is a link between the incident in the Netherlands and similar incidents in other countries.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 13 : Facebook and Instagram owner Meta challenged Britain's media regulator on Tuesday over how it calculates fees and potential fines under the Online Safety Act, arguing that the watchdog's methods are disproportionate. The 2023 law allows Ofcom to impose fines of up to 10 per cent of qualifying worldwide revenue, or £18 million ($23.9 million), whichever is greater, and to recover the costs of running its regime through fees calculated by reference to revenue. Meta's challenge comes a week after Ofcom opened an investigation into whether the company properly assessed the risks posed by its Instagram Instants feature before launching it in May. The case brought by Meta opened in London's High Court on Tuesday and centres on Ofcom's use of worldwide rather than UK revenue to determine fees and maximum potential fines.

Meta argued that Ofcom had exceeded its statutory powers by defining qualifying worldwide revenue as broadly as possible, with the objective of imposing the highest possible penalties. That was Ofcom's "overriding concern", Meta said in its legal submission. Meta is also challenging Ofcom's method of calculating fines where two or more providers owned by the same organisation are found jointly liable for breaches. Ofcom argues that its approach is proportionate and that it has struck a "careful balance" in defining qualifying revenue. Its court submission said that qualifying worldwide revenue was used only to calculate the maximum potential penalty and that any actual fine must be proportionate to the failure. Meta is also fighting Ofcom on other fronts. It joined TikTok and X in a separate legal hearing last week over the amount of information the regulator is demanding. Meta said it was committed to cooperating constructively with Ofcom. "However, we and others in the tech industry believe its decisions on the methodology to calculate fees and potential fines are disproportionate," a Meta spokesperson said. "We believe fees and penalties should be based on the services being regulated in the countries they're being regulated in. This would still allow Ofcom to impose the largest fines in UK corporate history." Ofcom said it had been tasked with regulating an industry that had been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years. An Ofcom spokesperson said Meta's case was one of a number of legal challenges it faced.  "On all these fronts, we will robustly defend our reasoning and decisions," the spokesperson said. ($1 = 0.7547 pounds)

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Oct 13 : An influential Hindu nationalist group close to India's ruling party urged the government on Tuesday to block Elon Musk's Starlink from launching satellite internet services in the country, citing national security concerns. Starlink's four-year wait to launch in India has come under renewed scrutiny after Musk last week accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and billionaire Mukesh Ambani of stalling its entry to favour Ambani's Reliance Jio. India's communications ministry said last week that security assessments were under way for Starlink and rival satellite ventures backed by Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. It described suggestions the approval process was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived". The call for Starlink's ban came from Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM), the economic wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist organisation that is the ideological parent of Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

If Washington imposes high tariffs on Indian imports "in the name of national security, then India is certainly within its rights to block Starlink based on its genuine national security concerns," national co-convenor Ashwani Mahajan said in a statement. Starlink's technology could make it difficult for authorities to restrict internet services during security emergencies and ensure Indian internet traffic passes through domestic infrastructure, Mahajan added. SJM has influenced Indian policy in recent years, notably pushing for rules to protect small traders from US-owned e-commerce firms Amazon and Walmart's Flipkart. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. MARKET WITH MORE THAN A BILLION INTERNET USERS Starlink is seeking to launch in a country with more than a billion internet subscribers. Alongside Starlink, satellite ventures backed by Reliance Jio and Bharti are awaiting final clearances to begin services. Musk has repeatedly taunted Ambani on X, questioning why Starlink still lacked a licence despite what he said were years of compliance with Indian requirements. Oct 13 : Bumble is set to go private in a $1.3 billion deal with Ithaca Holdings after struggling for years to revive growth, as a prolonged decline in users and shifting Gen Z dating habits batter the online dating industry. Shares of the company soared 56 per cent to $5.95 in early trading on Tuesday, after surging 50 per cent on Monday following media reports on the Ithaca deal. Bumble and larger rival Match, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have been battling declining user engagement, as younger users increasingly grow tired of swiping endlessly on apps and seek more organic ways to build connections. Match has so far outperformed Bumble with its portfolio of apps that cater to niche demographics, as well as international growth at Hinge, which draws users with its detailed, relationship-oriented profile formats.

"With Hinge having gained and continuing to gain share of more intentioned daters, Bumble's niche has eroded. The management, brand, and strategy changes have also not helped," said Chandler Willison, TMT Research Analyst at M Science. Bumble said Ithaca co-founders Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman will become Bumble's co-CEOs after the takeover. The firm has offered $6.05 per share for Bumble, representing a 122.4 per cent premium to the stock's closing price on June 24, a day before Reuters exclusively reported the company was exploring a sale. AI TOOLS YET TO SPUR RECOVERY Founded in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble pioneered the "women-first" approach to online dating that has been a defining feature for the company. But it rolled back the feature this year in a bid to improve its user retention rates. Under Herd, who returned as CEO in March 2025 after stepping down in 2023, the company has tried everything from raising prices and extending reply windows to adding AI tools that help users craft messages and exploring offline events to keep users hooked. It has also been testing a new AI matchmaking assistant in response to traditional swiping fatigue. But that has failed to aid its recovery. Total paying users fell 16.4 per cent to 3.2 million in the second quarter, while quarterly revenue has been declining for nearly two years. Bumble's market value has shrunk to about $582 million as of Monday's close, a far cry from its $14 billion valuation when it went public in 2021. Blackstone, which owns about 14 per cent of Bumble, according to LSEG data, and Herd have provided required shareholder approval for the deal.

Source: Reuters

Oct 13 : Agilent Technologies said on Tuesday it would acquire pathology software maker Proscia for $240 million in cash, plus up to $30 million tied to future performance targets, as the laboratory equipment maker expands its push into AI-enabled diagnostics. Here are some more details: • Privately held Proscia develops software that converts pathology slides into digital images that can be stored, reviewed and analyzed using artificial intelligence tools • Agilent said the acquisition would strengthen its pathology business and expand its presence in digital and AI-enabled diagnostics

Oct 13 : US online gambling operator BetMGM on Tuesday reported a 7 per cent rise in third-quarter revenue, driven by strong betting during the World Cup and a revamped sportsbook ahead of the NFL season.  • Shares of Ladbrokes-owner Entain rose 4 per cent after the update from BetMGM, a joint venture between Entain and US-based MGM Resorts • BetMGM reiterated its 2026 guidance, expecting net revenue toward the lower end of its $2.9 billion to $3.1 billion range and adjusted EBITDA toward the lower end of its $300 million to $350 million range • The company reported net revenue of $710 million for the three months ended September 30, up from $667 million a year earlier.

Oct 13 : Netflix said on Tuesday it had secured the rights to broadcast the 2030 World Cup in Spain, which is co-hosting the tournament, and Andorra. It would be Netflix's first broadcast of a major men's international tournament in Spain, the company said. The 2026 World Cup was aired there by national channel TVE. California-based Netflix did not disclose financial terms. Under the deal, one game per matchday will be free to watch in Spain. Netflix will also offer a national free-to-air channel which will broadcast a package of matches that includes all of Spain's games, both semi-finals and the final.

Netflix did not name the channel. TVE declined to comment on whether it would be interested in purchasing a package of matches. Spain, which won the World Cup in North America this year, will co-host the 2030 edition with Portugal and Morocco, although Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will stage inaugural matches marking the tournament's 100th anniversary. Uruguay hosted the first World Cup in 1930. Spain's state-owned television network TVE broadcast the Spanish national team's matches during this year's tournament, while private platform DAZN, which distributed Mediapro's pay-TV World Cup channel, showed all 104 games. Netflix holds the rights in the US and Canada for the 2027 Women's World Cup being hosted by Brazil and the 2031 edition being staged jointly by Costa Rica, Jamaica, Mexico and the US. The deal in Spain is more evidence of Netflix's push into the sports broadcasting world, with NFL, MLB, WWE, boxing and MMA all appearing on the streaming platform.

Source: Reuters

PARIS, Oct 13 : French investigators on Tuesday were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.    The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetise their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends. The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters. Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant trash containers on Tuesday. At least 350 supermarkets — a small fraction of the total number in France - were caught up in the strike.

FIRM BLAMES OUTDATED SOFTWARE The affected fridges relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss. On Monday, Danfoss said many of the affected units had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates" or were "running outdated firmware". It said it had "advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".  The company declined further comment on Tuesday. The serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of Danfoss' firmware have been known for months. On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses - since patched - in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices. 'BASIC CYBER HYGIENE' Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss' updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.  "This is about basic cyber hygiene," said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. "Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food." He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be "kids messing around". "If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet," he said. "No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience." PROBLEM STILL EXISTS Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Tuesday.  Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software.  Outdated and vulnerable versions were "still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces", Onyphe said.

Source: Reuters
